A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

in the absence of hypertension, longitudinal shortening contributes little to ejection fraction, and that in the presence of hypertension, longitudinal fiber shortening becomes a more important mechanism for ejection fraction than it is in the absence of arterial hypertension.
longitudinal shortening is an important contributor to ejection fraction only when the midwall shortens less than it does in normotensive individuals.
in the presence of arterial hypertention and an altered cardiac loading, the left ventricular ejection becomes a function of both the circumferential and the longitudinal fiber shortening.
The main takeaway from our work is that

in patients with hypertension, the long-axis shortens more than in normotensive patients, and that this mechanism is important in order to maintain an ejection fraction similar to that of normotensives.

the ejection fraction is determined primarily by circumferential wall shortening, but that longitudinal shortening becomes a compensatory mechanism in the presence of arterial pressure elevation and altered cardiac load.

longitudinal shortening is a major mechanism for ejection, and that it is important to measure it, especially in hypertensive subjects, in whom it may become an important compensatory mechanism for ejection.
